title: Hard negatives, the biggest training lever
summary: Random negatives produce a loss around 240,000 times smaller than hard ones, so they stop teaching almost immediately. Mining harder negatives is the biggest quality lever available, and it is also how you accidentally train your model that correct answers are wrong.
html:
Yesterday's in-batch negatives are free, and they are free because they are almost worthless. Today is about the most expensive part of building an embedding model, the part model cards rarely document, and the reason two models with identical architectures can differ by fifteen points of recall.

Watch the gradient disappear

Take the InfoNCE setup from Day 11 at temperature 0.05. One query, a positive at cosine 0.80, three negatives. Run it twice, changing only where the negatives came from:

random negatives   sims = [0.80, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05]
                   P(positive) = 1.00000    loss = 0.0000002

hard negatives     sims = [0.80, 0.78, 0.76, 0.70]
                   P(positive) = 0.44346    loss = 0.8131

The loss differs by a factor of roughly 240,000. The first example teaches the model essentially nothing. The forward pass ran, the backward pass ran, you paid for both, and the weights barely moved.

Worse, it gets rapidly worse as training proceeds. Hold the positive at 0.80 and vary how far the best random negative sits below it:

margin 0.30  ->  loss 0.003719
margin 0.50  ->  loss 0.000068
margin 0.65  ->  loss 0.000003
margin 0.80  ->  loss 0.000000

Early in training the margins are small and random negatives do real work. A few thousand steps in, the model can separate honey from TCP handshakes comfortably, the margin widens, and your entire batch of negatives stops contributing. You are now burning GPU hours to compute gradients that round to zero.

This has a familiar shape. It is the same problem as a benchmark suite where every test passes: the suite still runs, still costs time, and no longer tells you anything.

What counts as hard

A hard negative is a passage that scores high and is wrong. Not random, not topically distant. The ones that sit right next to the answer:

query:    "how do bees make honey?"

easy:     "TCP uses a three way handshake"          useless
mild:     "the queen lays up to 2000 eggs per day"  same document, wrong topic
hard:     "foragers collect nectar and add          same topic, adjacent step,
           invertase on the flight back"             does not answer the question

That third one is the Day 8 failure in reverse. It is what your system currently retrieves instead of the right chunk, so it is exactly what the model needs to be taught to rank lower.

Where to get them

Every method is the same move: run a retriever, take things it ranked highly, keep the ones that are not the labelled answer.

  • BM25 negatives. Retrieve lexically (Day 31), take high-ranking non-answers. Cheap, no GPU, and the original DPR work showed this alone was a large improvement over random. Still a sensible first move.
  • Self-mined dense negatives. Use the model you are currently training to retrieve, and take its own top-ranked mistakes. Sharper than BM25 because they target this model's specific weaknesses.
  • Cross-encoder filtered. Mine broadly, then score candidates with a stronger cross-encoder (Day 36) and keep the ones it confidently rates as non-relevant.

Self-mining creates a loop, because the model changes underneath you:

mine negatives with current model
  -> train
  -> model improves
  -> yesterday's hard negatives are now easy
  -> re-mine
  -> repeat

Notice what one turn of that loop costs. To mine from your corpus you first have to encode all of it, a full inference pass over every passage, then run a nearest neighbour search per training query. At a million passages that is not a preprocessing step you tuck into a setup script, it is a job comparable to building the production index itself. Then you discard the result and redo it a few thousand steps later.

ANCE made this explicit by refreshing the negative index asynchronously during training. The engineering problem is that re-encoding a corpus mid-training is expensive, so you refresh every N steps and accept that your negatives are always slightly stale. That is a scheduling and throughput tradeoff, and it is the kind of thing that decides whether a training run takes three days or three weeks.

The trap that quietly ruins models

Here is the part to be careful about, because it is the failure mode you will actually hit.

You mine the top 100 passages and discard the labelled positive. What is left is not negatives. It is everything that was not labelled, and those are different things.

Retrieval datasets are labelled sparsely. MS MARCO typically marks one relevant passage per query out of millions. In a corpus that size, other passages answer the question perfectly well and simply never got annotated. Your miner, doing its job, ranks those highly. They land in your negative set.

Now look at what InfoNCE does with a false negative. The loss pushes the query away from a passage that genuinely answers it. You are not failing to teach the model something. You are actively teaching it the opposite, with a large gradient, because false negatives score high and high-scoring negatives dominate the update at low temperature. The mechanism that makes hard negatives valuable is the same mechanism that makes false negatives harmful.

Three mitigations, in the order most people apply them:

  • Skip the top. Do not mine from ranks 1 to 10, start at 20 or 30. Crude, costs you your hardest genuine negatives, takes one line.
  • Margin threshold. Discard candidates scoring within some distance of the positive, on the theory that a near-tie is more likely mislabelled than genuinely hard.
  • Cross-encoder denoising. Score candidates with a stronger model and drop anything it thinks is relevant. This is what RocketQA introduced and it is the approach that works best. It also costs a second model and an inference pass over every candidate.

Why this is under-documented

Two models can share an architecture, a pooling strategy, a temperature and a batch size, and differ substantially in quality. The difference is usually the negatives, and it is usually the thing the model card says least about. You will find the batch size stated proudly and the negative mining described as "hard negatives" with no further detail.

So when you compare embedding models on Day 14 and one wins, you generally will not be able to explain why from published information. Measure on your own data and accept that the mechanism is opaque. That is an honest limitation of the field rather than a gap in your reading.

You now know how these models are trained. What remains is a detail of how you are meant to call them, one that costs recall silently and catches almost everyone once. Tomorrow: query and passage asymmetry.
exercise:
1. Reproduce the saturation curve. Fix a positive at 0.80 and sweep the best negative from 0.78 down to 0.10, computing the InfoNCE loss at T=0.05 at each step. Plot it or just print it. Find the margin at which the loss drops below 0.001, because past that point those examples are costing you compute and returning nothing.

2. Mine hard negatives from your own corpus. Use your Day 8 TF-IDF scorer as the miner. Pick a question you know the answer to, retrieve the top 10, and remove the correct chunk. Read what is left. Those are your hard negatives, and looking at them tells you what your retriever currently confuses.

3. Find a false negative. In that same top 10, look for a chunk that actually answers the question but is not the one you had in mind. If you find one, you have just reproduced the exact failure this lesson warns about, on your own data, in under a minute. If you do not, try a broader question.
